entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Du Qiong (courtesy name Boyu), who died in 250 CE, was a distinguished official, astronomer, and diviner whose career spanned the tumultuous early to mid-period of the Three Kingdoms era in China. Serving the state of Shu Han, founded by Liu Bei, Du Qiong embodied the classical Chinese ideal of a scholar-official adept in both practical administration and esoteric knowledge, particularly in celestial observation and prognostication. His work was critical in maintaining the calendrical system and offering cosmic counsel to a nascent state striving for legitimacy and stability amidst intense geopolitical fragmentation.

Du Qiong's primary contributions lay in his dual roles as an astronomer and a diviner. He was appointed as Grand Astrologer (Taishi Ling) by Liu Bei, a position of immense importance in ancient Chinese courts, responsible for observing celestial phenomena, interpreting omens, and formulating the calendar—a fundamental aspect of imperial authority. His expertise in the "Changes of the Stars" (Xingzhan) allowed him to advise the Shu Han leadership, including the emperor and the regent Zhuge Liang, on auspicious timings for military campaigns and state affairs. Beyond his celestial duties, Du Qiong also held administrative posts, demonstrating the versatile demands placed upon learned officials during this period of state-building.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Du Qiong's role as Grand Astrologer and diviner was crucial for maintaining calendrical accuracy and providing cosmic legitimacy to the nascent Shu Han state, influencing its strategic decision-making and contributing to the continuity of scientific tradition amidst political upheaval.
